Count nearby words and explain their association

Source: vignettes/collocation-association.Rmd
collocation-association.Rmd

A word can occur near a node often simply because it is common. To describe association, compare the observed number of pairs with an expected number computed from an explicit population of possible pairs. Keep both counts: a high association score from one occurrence deserves different interpretation from a frequently repeated combination.

This guide uses ldfreq 0.3.0.9010 or later and optional quanteda >= 4.5.0. It starts with adjacent words, then expands to a left/right span. The two helpers in examples/collocation.R use the saved searches from examples/concordance.R. These are explicitly sourced, installed examples, not exported functions. The examples below are authored for hand checking; they are not learner data or an assessment of annotation accuracy.

Start with a complete, source-linked search 

library(ldfreq)

demo <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "collocation-demo.R",
  package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), demo)
helper <- demo$helper
search <- demo$search
print(demo$annotations$segments, row.names = FALSE)
#>  document_id segment_id      text token_count
#>           d1         s1 a b a b c           5
#>           d2         s1   a c b a           4
#>           d2         s2       b a           2
#>          gap         s1     a , b           3
#>      missing         s1   a gap b           3
#>        empty         s1                     0
#>                                                       text_sha256
#>  d110393ed7da5c855423fe9e64e7bac0559ce7da85188465544cfb28fe23e0cb
#>  61312e7448895df2363ff3c60711105fdb4b61bb92389627331e76c067160a3a
#>  beedb4a7ba34c4ea09727022655dd743d5dda2940f1c8e4ec56ff2904324026c
#>  d33dc101d06f8d7fee912c714d098f98f64aed510d78774d6fa632967ce5a892
#>  8e964a33b68f627c79b0409ec2adfa9ec2af20baae5d7a0815fc9a3f61e53bc0
#>  e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855

The imported tokens retain original positions and character offsets. The chosen lemma column is missing for gap; the comma is explicitly excluded. d2 has two separate segments. Every segment is a hard boundary. A segment means a sentence only when your input defines it as one; the helper does not split sentences automatically.

For your own unchanged lexdiv_import_annotations() result, source both helpers and make a search. See the concordance guide for preparing aligned annotations from your text or parser output.

helper <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
for (file in c("concordance.R", "collocation.R"))
  sys.source(system.file("examples", file, package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), helper)
search <- helper$concordance_search(annotations, list(node = "learn"),
  term_col = "lemma", keep = keep, window = 5L)
nearby <- helper$collocation_profile(search, "node", span = c(left = 3L, right = 3L))

A node query must have one token pattern. Fixed, wildcard and regular-expression queries retain their saved search settings. A pattern matching several forms pools those node positions into one class. Context terms use exact UTF-8 values of the selected column: the node’s case-insensitive matching does not merge context forms such as Word and word. No new case or Unicode normalization is performed. Specify and preserve any normalization in the annotations.

Adjacent words: inspect the denominator first 

adjacent <- helper$collocation_profile(search, "a") # L0/R1
print(adjacent$results, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
#>  context observed node_marginal context_marginal opportunities expected     MI
#>        b        2             3                3             8    1.125 0.8301
#>        a        0             3                3             8    1.125   -Inf
#>        c        1             3                2             8    0.750 0.4150
#>  t_score documents context_documents meets_min_count        status
#>   0.6187         1                 2            TRUE            ok
#>       NA         0                 2           FALSE zero_observed
#>   0.2500         1                 2            TRUE            ok
print(adjacent$documents, row.names = FALSE)
#>  document_id source_tokens kept_tokens searchable_tokens missing_terms
#>           d1             5           5                 5             0
#>           d2             6           6                 6             0
#>          gap             3           2                 2             0
#>      missing             3           3                 2             1
#>        empty             0           0                 0             0
#>  node_occurrences candidate_slot_pairs eligible_pairs excluded_pairs node_pairs
#>                 2                    4              4              0          2
#>                 3                    4              4              0          1
#>                 1                    2              0              2          0
#>                 1                    2              0              2          0
#>                 0                    0              0              0          0
#>  nodes_with_context            status
#>                   2                ok
#>                   1                ok
#>                   0 no_eligible_pairs
#>                   0 no_eligible_pairs
#>                   0 no_eligible_pairs

There are 8 eligible adjacent pairs, of which 3 start at the node a. The context b appears at the right endpoint of 3 eligible pairs, and the pair a b occurs 2 times. Thus its expected count is 3 * 3 / 8 = 1.125. These marginals count positions in eligible pairs, not unrestricted unigram frequencies. Final tokens, excluded endpoints and segment boundaries affect the denominator.

For each context type, the result includes:

Column Meaning in the saved pair population
observed Pairs with both a matching node and this context term, O
node_marginal All pairs whose node endpoint matches the query, R
context_marginal All pairs whose context endpoint has this term, C
opportunities All eligible ordered pairs, N
expected R × C / N, E
MI Pointwise mutual information, log2(O / E)
t_score (O − E) / sqrt(O)
documents Distinct documents contributing to O
context_documents Distinct documents contributing to C
meets_min_count Display-selection flag; counts remain complete
status ok, zero_observed, or no_node_opportunities

The MI and t-score definitions follow Evert’s association-measure discussion, Sections 4.1–4.3. MI is sensitive to rare combinations; report O and choose a frequency threshold explicitly. Here t-score is a descriptive association measure, not a Student t statistic or a significance test. Overlapping windows share tokens, and documents may share writers; these rows are not independent observations for a study-level model.

The helper applies no smoothing. When O = 0 and E > 0, MI is -Inf and t-score is NA (zero_observed). When no eligible pair starts at a matching node, E = 0 and both scores are NA (no_node_opportunities). With no eligible pairs at all, the results table is empty and document status explains why. Only context types present in eligible pairs receive rows. An absent row is not a claim of zero frequency in an external corpus, and a missing lemma is not a known zero.

Expand the span without changing the meaning of a position 

span <- helper$collocation_profile(search, "a", span = c(left = 2L, right = 2L))
print(span$results, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
#>  context observed node_marginal context_marginal opportunities expected      MI
#>        b        8            13               12            30    5.200  0.6215
#>        a        2            13               13            30    5.633 -1.4940
#>        c        3            13                5            30    2.167  0.4695
#>  t_score documents context_documents meets_min_count status
#>   0.9899         4                 4            TRUE     ok
#>  -2.5692         1                 4            TRUE     ok
#>   0.4811         2                 2            TRUE     ok
print(span$documents[c("document_id", "candidate_slot_pairs",
  "eligible_pairs", "excluded_pairs", "node_occurrences", "nodes_with_context", "node_pairs")],
  row.names = FALSE)
#>  document_id candidate_slot_pairs eligible_pairs excluded_pairs
#>           d1                   14             14              0
#>           d2                   12             12              0
#>          gap                    6              2              4
#>      missing                    6              2              4
#>        empty                    0              0              0
#>  node_occurrences nodes_with_context node_pairs
#>                 2                  2          6
#>                 3                  3          5
#>                 1                  1          1
#>                 1                  1          1
#>                 0                  0          0

The span example has 30 eligible ordered pairs. Each ordered pair of original positions within the requested distance is one opportunity. Both endpoints must be searchable, and they must belong to the same segment. The span includes all distances from 1 to the chosen width on each side; left = 0 or right = 0 selects only the other direction.

These rules determine the counts:

  • A node token cannot pair with itself. Two occurrences of the same word can pair with each other. With both directions enabled, (i, j) and (j, i) are separate ordered opportunities.
  • Repeated context tokens each count. Two node tokens may pair with the same context token: their original position pairs are different.
  • Excluded or missing endpoints cannot form a pair. Intervening excluded or missing slots still consume distance and do not block a wider-span pair. Thus a , b can contribute at distance +2, but never at +1. Splitting the input into sentence segments is the way to prohibit sentence crossing.
  • Node and context marginals and N are recounted over this whole pair population. Do not substitute corpus unigram totals, or multiply the node frequency by twice the span: boundaries and endpoint availability matter.
  • Left and right distances are pooled within a call. To describe one side, run a separate call with the other width zero; filtering the saved pairs afterward would invalidate the original scores and denominators.

This is an independence model for the two roles in a population of ordered token pairs. It is not the conventional surface-window approximation using unigram frequencies times span width. Scores from tools using different populations or exclusion rules need not agree.

The complete $pairs table contains background opportunities as well as matching node pairs. $documents retains empty and zero-match documents, original/searchable/missing token counts, candidate and eligible pair counts, node occurrences, and nodes with at least one eligible context. By default, max_pairs = 1e6 bounds all candidate slot pairs before endpoint exclusions. Exceeding the bound raises an error rather than truncating the sample. This is not a full memory bound or a streaming large-corpus engine.

Select frequent combinations and return to their source 

selected <- helper$collocation_profile(search, "a", min_count = 2L)
shown <- subset(selected$results, meets_min_count)
shown <- shown[order(-shown$MI, -shown$observed), ]
print(shown, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
#>  context observed node_marginal context_marginal opportunities expected     MI
#>        b        2             3                3             8    1.125 0.8301
#>  t_score documents context_documents meets_min_count status
#>   0.6187         1                 2            TRUE     ok

min_count is a positive whole number. It sets a flag; it never removes pairs, changes marginals, or overwrites below-threshold counts. The default of 1 includes singletons for inspection and is not a recommendation for ranking rare combinations. Choose a threshold appropriate to your corpus and report it.

pairs <- subset(span$pairs, is_node & context_term == "b")
kwic <- span$search$occurrences[
  match(pairs$occurrence_id, span$search$occurrences$occurrence_id), ]
inspection <- data.frame(document_id = pairs$document_id,
  segment_id = pairs$segment_id, node_position = pairs$node_position,
  context_position = pairs$context_position, distance = pairs$distance,
  pre = kwic$pre, node = kwic$keyword, post = kwic$post,
  context = span$search$source$tokens$surface[pairs$context_row])
print(inspection, row.names = FALSE)
#>  document_id segment_id node_position context_position distance  pre node
#>           d1         s1             1                2        1         a
#>           d1         s1             3                2       -1 a b     a
#>           d1         s1             3                4        1 a b     a
#>           d2         s1             1                3        2         a
#>           d2         s1             4                3       -1 c b     a
#>           d2         s2             2                1       -1   b     a
#>          gap         s1             1                3        2         a
#>      missing         s1             1                3        2         a
#>    post context
#>     b a       b
#>     b c       b
#>     b c       b
#>     c b       b
#>               b
#>               b
#>     , b       b
#>   gap b       b

Each matching pair links to a saved node occurrence ID, original token rows and segment-local, 1-based inclusive character offsets. A node KWIC may appear more than once because it contributed several pairs. Its display window comes from the original search; choose a search window at least as wide as the collocation span to see all the context in this display. The full original segment remains available even with a narrower KWIC window.

Save the complete record and replay it 

record <- list(adjacent = adjacent, span = span, session = sessionInfo())
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") # use a durable project path for your analysis
saveRDS(record, file, version = 2)
reopened <- readRDS(file)
helper$collocation_validate(reopened$span)
replayed <- helper$collocation_profile(reopened$span$search, "a",
  span = reopened$span$settings$span)
stopifnot(identical(replayed, reopened$span))
unlink(file)

Retain the full object, source annotations, helper/package versions and session information; a CSV of selected scores cannot reconstruct the denominator. collocation_validate() detects accidental changes to the saved record, including its search. It is not an authenticity check for supplied annotations. Exact whole-object replay requires the same package version; after an upgrade, compare counts and settings explicitly instead of assuming object identity.

What was checked, and what the scores do not establish

The authored example’s adjacent pairs agree with lexdiv_ngrams(). A separate Cartesian enumeration verifies the pair sets and 2×2 tables for left-only, right-only and two-sided spans, including segment boundaries, repeated nodes, excluded endpoints and missing terms. Positive-count scores were checked against corpora 0.7’s am.score() with the same positional marginals and span.size = 1: the span is already represented by the pair population. The deliberate NA t-score convention at O = 0 is checked separately. corpora is not needed to run these helpers.

These checks concern counting and numerical reproduction on constructed data. They do not validate idiomaticity, semantic cohesion, language proficiency, or performance on a natural corpus. Phrase nodes, dependency relations and automatic sentence detection are outside this example. The existing n-gram reference profiles retain their own frequency and coverage contracts; a pruned reference table cannot supply missing marginals. Preserve writer, task and occasion identifiers when relating text measures to research outcomes, as in the repeated-observations guide.
